<PubmedArticle><MedlineCitation Status="MEDLINE" Owner="NLM" IndexingMethod="Automated"><PMID Version="1">42993313</PMID><DateCompleted><Year>2026</Year><Month>11</Month><Day>06</Day></DateCompleted><DateRevised><Year>2026</Year><Month>11</Month><Day>06</Day></DateRevised><Article PubModel="Electronic"><Journal><ISSN IssnType="Electronic">1248-9204</ISSN><JournalIssue CitedMedium="Internet"><Volume>31</Volume><Issue>1</Issue><PubDate><Year>2026</Year><Month>Nov</Month><Day>06</Day></PubDate></JournalIssue><Title>Hernia : the journal of hernias and abdominal wall surgery</Title><ISOAbbreviation>Hernia</ISOAbbreviation></Journal><ArticleTitle>Postpartum repair of umbilical hernias following conservative management during pregnancy: a retrospective cohort study.</ArticleTitle><ELocationID EIdType="pii" ValidYN="Y">3</ELocationID><ELocationID EIdType="doi" ValidYN="Y">10.1007/s10029-026-03852-y</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText Label="BACKGROUND" NlmCategory="BACKGROUND">The optimal timing of elective umbilical hernia repair following conservative management during pregnancy remains controversial. Physiological postpartum changes, including persistent abdominal wall laxity and elevated intra-abdominal pressure, may influence surgical outcomes and recurrence risk. This study evaluated the clinical outcomes and impact of surgical timing on postpartum umbilical hernia repair.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="METHODS">A retrospective cohort study was conducted at a tertiary referral center between January 2010 and December 2018. Pregnant women diagnosed with umbilical hernia were initially managed conservatively unless emergent intervention was required. Patients subsequently underwent elective open mesh repair during the postpartum period. Primary outcome was hernia recurrence. Secondary outcomes included operative time, length of hospital stay (LOS), postoperative pain assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), and perioperative complications. Statistical analysis was performed using ANOVA, Chi-square, and Fisher's exact tests.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="RESULTS">A total of 114 women underwent elective postpartum umbilical hernia repair following conservative management during pregnancy. Mean age was [Formula: see text] years, and mean BMI was 38.8&#xa0;kg/m&#xb2;, with most patients classified as obese and multiparous. Overall recurrence rate was 3.5% (n&#x2009;=&#x2009;4). All recurrences occurred either in patients undergoing early repair (&lt;&#x2009;6 months postpartum) or in those who became pregnant within one year after surgery. Delayed repair was associated with significantly improved perioperative outcomes. Mean operative time decreased from 145&#xa0;min in the early repair group to 91&#xa0;min in patients repaired after 24 months postpartum (p&#x2009;&lt;&#x2009;0.001). Mean LOS decreased from 49 to 30&#xa0;h (p&#x2009;&lt;&#x2009;0.001). Patients undergoing delayed repair also demonstrated significantly lower postoperative pain scores (VAS 3.2 vs. 6.8, p&#x2009;&lt;&#x2009;0.001) and reduced postoperative complication rates. No recurrences were observed in women who delayed subsequent pregnancy for more than two years after repair.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="CONCLUSIONS">Elective postpartum umbilical hernia repair following conservative management during pregnancy is safe and associated with favorable perioperative outcomes. Delayed repair was associated with reduced operative complexity, postoperative pain, and complications. Although recurrence events were observed predominantly after early repair or subsequent early pregnancy, larger prospective studies are required to clarify the relationship between repair timing and recurrence risk.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>&#xa9; 2026.
